question: In recent months, a number of Spanish autonomous regions have been drawing up and publishing rules that breach the EU framework on the free movement of workers and services, particularly with regard to the regulation of sports professions. In the light of the above: 1.

Taking into account that other Member States such as Ireland and France (Certificats de qualification professionnelle – CQP) provide for the profession of personal trainer to be practised by holders of a professional certification managed by a European register of professionals, which is recognised by the Commission itself, can a Spanish law (in Madrid, Valencia, Murcia, Extremadura, Castile and León or Navarra) which limits the exercise of that profession exclusively to people with a university degree be regarded as a restriction on free competition (movement of workers and services)?

Could laws of that kind be considered incompatible with the objectives of the European Union as expressed in Article 1 of Regulation (EU) 2019/128 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 16 January 2019 establishing a European Centre for the Development of Vocational Training (Cedefop)?
answer: Member States have the competence to regulate access to and pursuit of professions in accordance with EU law, while EU citizens have the right to freedom of establishment and to the free provision of services under the Treaty on the Functioning of the EU (TFEU) (1).

Thus, regulations must be justified, proportionate, and non-discriminatory, with a proportionality assessment conducted before adopting or amending any professional regulations, as stipulated by Directive (EU) 2018/958 on a proportionality test (2).

Grounds like public interest protection can justify access restrictions to sports professions, but it is crucial to ensure fair competition and accessibility for qualified individuals across the EU. The Regulated Professions Database (3) lists regulated professions notified by Member States but does not confer rights to citizens.

Personal trainers and other sports professionals seeking employment in another Member State have the right to free movement as workers under EU law, which prohibits discrimination. National rules on access to regulated professions must apply equally to nationals and EU citizens.

Article 45 of the TFEU and Regulation (EU) 492/2011 on the freedom of movement for workers within the EU (4) are directly applicable, allowing workers to invoke these rights before national authorities and courts if their rights are not respected.

Regarding the compatibility of regulations reserving access to professional activities with Article 1 of Regulation (EU) 2019/128 (5), it is important to note that this regulation does not address the regulation of professions. Instead, it establishes the framework for the European Centre for the Development of Vocational Training.
